title: Payal Kapadia Chaired a Cannes Jury. Then She Handed the Top Prize to a French Debut. The Symbolism Was Not Lost on Anyone.
excerpt: The first Indian to preside over the Critics' Week jury, Kapadia used her platform to champion first-time filmmakers — the same ecosystem that launched her own career from a Pune film school to the Grand Prix.
body:
Two years ago, Payal Kapadia stood on the stage at Cannes holding the Grand Prix — the festival's second-highest honor — for All We Imagine as Light. She became the first Asian director in the festival's modern era to receive it. Last year, she sat on the main competition jury, watching other filmmakers compete for the same prizes she had won.

This year, she came back as the boss.

The 65th Critics' Week at Cannes, which ran from May 13 to 21 as part of the 79th Cannes Film Festival, was presided over by Kapadia as jury president. She is the first Indian filmmaker to hold this position in the section's history. The appointment placed her at the head of a jury that included Canadian actor Theodore Pellerin, French musician Oklou, Ghanaian-British producer Ama Ampadu, and Bangkok World Film Festival head Donsaron Kovitvanitcha.

## What She Said — And Why It Mattered

Kapadia's statement upon accepting the role carried a weight that went beyond ceremony. "At a time when independent cinema is being eroded in every country, supporting the first works of filmmakers is almost a form of resistance to market forces," she said. "First movies are often freer, more daring and fearless, told with an individual voice, and to champion those is absolutely essential."

The word "resistance" was deliberate. In an industry where Indian independent cinema increasingly struggles to find screens — squeezed between Bollywood's star-driven machinery and the algorithmic curation of streaming platforms — Kapadia was making a case not just for festival cinema but for the structural ecosystem that makes it possible.

## The Awards

Under Kapadia's jury, the AMI Paris Grand Prize went to La Gradiva, the debut feature by French cinematographer Marine Atlan. The film follows a group of French students on a field trip to Naples, where one young man also goes searching for his heritage. The Louis Roederer Foundation Rising Star Award went to Spanish actress-turned-director Aina Clotet for Viva, which traces a woman's life reassessment after a cancer diagnosis.

Chinese director Zou Jing's A Girl Unknown won the Gan Foundation Award for Distribution. The SACD Award for best screenplay was shared by director Blerta Basholli and co-writer Nicole Borgeat for the coming-of-age drama Dua.

## The Larger Indian Moment at Cannes

Kapadia's jury presidency was part of a broader Indian presence at the 79th festival. The Critics' Week section specifically focuses on first and second features — the exact category that launched Kapadia's own career when her short film Afternoon Clouds premiered at Cannes in 2017. Her documentary A Night of Knowing Nothing won the Golden Eye in 2021 in the Directors' Fortnight. The trajectory from selected filmmaker to jury president in under a decade is almost without precedent in Indian cinema.

"My own journey as a filmmaker was supported early on because of film festival selections," Kapadia said in an interview with Hollywood Reporter India. "Through these I had the opportunity to meet others like myself from across the world and helped me build a community of future collaborators."

## What It Means for the Diaspora

For NRI audiences who follow Indian cinema beyond box office tracking, Kapadia represents something genuinely new — an Indian filmmaker whose international reputation was built entirely outside the commercial film industry. She did not come up through Bollywood. She did not need a star-driven project to earn global recognition. Her path ran through FTII Pune, independent production, documentary filmmaking, and festival circuits.

That path is now institutional. When the most prestigious parallel section at the world's most important film festival hands its jury presidency to an Indian filmmaker trained at a government film school, it sends a message about what kind of Indian cinema the global industry takes seriously. It is not the cinema of 500 crore budgets and pan-India releases. It is the cinema of personal vision, rigorous craft, and stories that mainstream distributors overlook.

Kapadia has not announced her next directorial project. But with a Grand Prix, a jury presidency, and an Academy membership now on her resume, whatever she makes next will arrive with a level of international attention that few Indian filmmakers have ever commanded.

The question for India's film ecosystem is whether it can create more filmmakers like her — or whether she remains a singular exception in a system that rewards formula over risk.
author: Diaspora Desk
